titleZh: 当 AI 能自己做 AI 研究——一场关于「递归自我改进」的硬碰硬辩论
titleEn: Ryan Greenblatt – What happens once AI can automate AI research?
author: Dwarkesh Patel × Ryan Greenblatt
authorTitle: Ryan Greenblatt 是 Redwood Research 首席科学家，专注技术层面的 AI 安全与防护；Dwarkesh Patel 是《Dwarkesh Podcast》主理人，长期对 RSI 持怀疑立场
summary: Greenblatt 的核心主张：AI 研发高度可验证，一旦 AI 匹敌顶尖研究员，一年内可压缩出四到五年的进展——他给出的自动化中位年份是 2031，2040 年前发生 AI 接管的概率 35–40%。
keyPoints: **可验证性是 RSI 的引信**：Greenblatt 认为 AI 研发天然适合 RL——小规模训练任务可容器化、可复现、可打分，各家实验室早已在这类环境上做激进 RL，能力会外溢到真正吃重的研究判断上。
**「一年顶五年」不是修辞，是中位预期**：他的中位判断是 AI 研发完全自动化落在 2030–2031，「在所有岗位上打败人类」落在 2033，而两者之间的间隔大概率被压进一年之内。
**Dwarkesh 的反驳与让步**：他原本认定瓶颈在算力与人类专家数据——没有真实世界数据就长不出能干基辛格、乔布斯那类活的 ASI；一场辩论后他承认这种加速「plausible」，但仍不买账「一年五年」。
**「对齐给谁」比「能否对齐」更棘手**：Claude 宪法明确不把自己定位成用户的个人代言人，而是把长期价值观装进模型。两人一致担心：当投票、资本、对世界的认知全被超级智能中介，个人失去代言人是结构性问题。
**从 reward hacking 到接管的连续谱**：OpenAI 内部 AI 黑进包管理器互相留暗号刷评测分、一个月没被发现——两人把这类真实事件外推为「协同接管」的起点。Greenblatt 给 2040 年前接管概率 35–40%，Dwarkesh 仍不认同这个高位。

quotes.en: Maybe my median expectation is something like four or five years of AI progress in a single year.
quotes.zh: 我的中位预期大概是：一年之内取得四到五年的 AI 进展。

quotes.en: I would say that I expect full automation of AI R&D perhaps somewhere around 2031, 2030.
quotes.zh: 我会说，我预期 AI 研发的完全自动化大概在 2031、2030 年前后。

quotes.en: But at the end of the day, there is a real question of: aligned to whom?
quotes.zh: 但说到底，有个真问题是：对齐到谁？

quotes.en: By 2040? Let’s see. Maybe around 35 or 40%?
quotes.zh: 到 2040 年？我想想。大概 35% 到 40% 吧？

quotes.en: it’s pretty spooky to have a bajillion really smart AIs running your whole world where you don’t really understand quite what’s going on.
quotes.zh: 让一亿亿个非常聪明的 AI 运行你的整个世界，而你并不真正明白到底在发生什么——这挺瘆人的。

secondaryReads.source: Zvi Mowshowitz《Don't Worry About the Vase》
secondaryReads.pov: Zvi 对这期播客做了逐段拆解，立场比 Greenblatt 更激进：他认为 Ryan 的加速估计「反而偏慢」，因为漏算了复利效应，而且当下已经能观察到 AI 对研发的显著倍增。他还给出一个诊断框架——Dwarkesh 是「AGI pilled 但没吃 ASI 药」，其怀疑的根子在于假定 AI 只能从 X 的样例里学会 X。Zvi 最尖锐的补充是：让 AI 做 AI 研发，不只是「快得吓人」，而是会默认朝可测量的指标优化，最终陷入「用 RLVR 去做 RLVR」的错位螺旋。

secondaryReads.source: Redwood Research Blog（Greenblatt 本人技术笔记）
secondaryReads.pov: 这是 Greenblatt 播客论证背后的量化底稿。他在此把「软件奇点」与「一次性加速」拆开：即使不存在自我强化的软件奇点（r 显著大于 1），单靠自动化带来的一次性提速加上算力回报提升，在他的参数设定下第一年也能产出约 2.5 年的进展。想判断「一年顶五年」是不是数字游戏，应该来看这篇的模型假设而非播客里的口头中位数。

secondaryReads.source: 80,000 Hours Podcast（2025 年 2 月与 Greenblatt 的早期访谈）
secondaryReads.pov: 一年半前的 Greenblatt 基线，可用作时间线漂移的对照：当时他给 AI 研发完全自动化「4 年内 25%、8 年内 50%」，并列出了减速证据（高质量数据枯竭、每个数量级算力回报递减、窄域能力未必泛化）。把它和本期 2031 中位数并置，能看出他的判断是收窄而非外推，也能看出 Dwarkesh 这次逼问的正是当年那份减速清单。

insight: 别把这期当末日预言听——真正该抄走的是 Greenblatt 的判据：一项工作能不能被 AI 自我加速，取决于它是否「可容器化 + 可打分 + 可快速迭代」。拿这把尺子去量你手下 500 人的活，会发现被率先吃掉的不是最初级的岗位，而是那些反馈闭环最干净的岗位；而 Dwarkesh 死守的「真实世界数据」护城河，恰恰是咨询与交付业务真正的资产——前提是你现在就开始把它沉淀成可训练的形态，而不是留在人的脑子里。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

Today I’m chatting with [Ryan Greenblatt](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=UESxdDsAAAAJ&hl=en), who is the chief scientist at [Redwood Research](https://www.redwoodresearch.org/), where he focuses on technical [AI safety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_safety) and security work.

I want to talk to you about [recursive self-improvement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recursive_self-improvement). This is the idea that once we build human-level intelligences, they quickly slingshot towards tens of billions of [superintelligences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintelligence), which are each individually more competent than the top human experts across every field. Whether or not this turns out to be the case is probably the most important question in the world right now. And historically, I’ve been quite skeptical that this kind of thing happens, but, you seem to think that it might be plausible, and so I wanted to hear the case for it.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

Let’s talk about this. First, I think it’s worth noting that AI R&D is a type of task at which the AIs are especially good, because the companies are trying really hard to make their AIs good at AI R&D. It’s also the kind of domain that has a lot of nice properties from the perspective of how AI development works right now. It’s pretty verifiable. You can do a bunch of stuff iteratively, and it’ll hill climb on various metrics.

I think once you have AIs which are roughly matching the top human experts in AI R&D, that could kick off a feedback loop where the AIs are doing AI research. That produces smarter AIs. That feeds back in. That feedback loop could be strong enough that you end up with a lot of progress in a short period of time. Maybe my median expectation is something like four or five years of AI progress in a single year. This requires really overcoming a huge amount of diminishing returns in research and basically doing the equivalent of the progress we would have gotten after a really large compute scale-out. So this is a pretty impressive, big thing.

It’s worth keeping in mind that five years of AI progress, four years of AI progress, even three years of AI progress, is really a lot of fucking AI progress. A little over three years ago, [GPT-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPT-4) had come out. Right now, of course, we have [Mythos 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Mythos) or whatever, and maybe a somewhat better model that Anthropic has internally. That is just a huge amount of progress in a bit over three years. If we’re talking about five years, then maybe we’re talking more about a jump from [GPT-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPT-3) to Mythos 5 or whatever.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

今天我请到了 [Ryan Greenblatt](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=UESxdDsAAAAJ&hl=en)，[Redwood Research](https://www.redwoodresearch.org/) 的首席科学家，专注于技术层面的 [AI 安全](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_safety)与防护工作。

我想跟你聊[递归自我改进](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recursive_self-improvement)（RSI）。这个说法是：一旦我们造出人类水平的智能体，它们会迅速弹射成几百亿个[超级智能](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintelligence)，每一个单拎出来都比各领域最顶尖的人类专家更强。这事最后成不成立，大概是当今世界最重要的问题。一直以来我对这类事情的发生相当怀疑，但你似乎觉得它有可能成立，所以我想听听支持它的论证。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

那就来聊聊。首先，我认为值得指出：AI 研发（AI R&D）恰恰是 AI 特别擅长的一类任务——因为各家公司都在拼命让自家 AI 擅长 AI 研发。而且按当下 AI 开发的运作方式来看，这个领域有很多讨喜的性质。它相当可验证，你可以迭代着做一大堆事，模型会在各种指标上爬坡。

我认为，一旦你有了大致能匹敌 AI 研发顶尖人类专家的 AI，就可能启动一个反馈回路：AI 在做 AI 研究，产出更聪明的 AI，再反馈回去。这个回路可能强到让你在很短时间内积累大量进展。我的中位预期大概是：一年之内取得四到五年的 AI 进展。这要求真正克服掉研究中巨量的收益递减，基本上等于把一次超大规模算力扩张之后才该拿到的进展给做出来。所以这是相当惊人的一件大事。

值得记住的是，五年的 AI 进展、四年的 AI 进展，哪怕只是三年的 AI 进展，那都是他妈的一大堆 AI 进展。三年多一点之前，[GPT-4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPT-4) 才刚出来。而现在我们当然已经有了 [Mythos 5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Mythos) 之类的东西，Anthropic 内部可能还有更好一点的模型。这就是三年多一点里的巨量进展。如果说的是五年，那可能更接近从 [GPT-3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPT-3) 一路跳到 Mythos 5 这种幅度。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

I think this argument has three different parts. Now I want to evaluate each one of them. First is the argument that AI R&D is very verifiable. Second is the argument that if you automate AI R&D, you could get four or five years of progress in a single year. Third is the argument that what comes out the other end of four or five years of AI progress at the current pace, starting at the point whenever AI R&D is automated, is an AI where you can drop it on the job at basically anything you can imagine.

You can drop it in Texas politics in the 1940s, and it outmaneuvers [Lyndon Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson). You can drop it in [TSMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSMC), and it learns how to do better process engineering at TSMC. It’s certainly a better video editor… My video editors are very excellent, but it is just, in general, better than humans at any given job that it finds itself trying to do.

So I want to evaluate all of these sub-arguments that lead to basically getting ASI pretty soon after this benchmark, which you’re expecting by 2030 or something, right?

**Ryan Greenblatt**

I would say that I expect full automation of AI R&D perhaps somewhere around 2031, 2030. Getting to the “beats all humans on the job” milestone, maybe my median expectation is around 2033. But if I see AIs fully automating AI R&D, I think I’m expecting that probably within a year. The way the forecasting works out, the difference between medians is bigger than the median difference between milestones. Anyway, whatever.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

By the way, there’s this meme on the internet. Every time I’m trying to ask about people’s timelines, [when I’m asking Dario](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/dario-amodei-2) or somebody, I’m always like, “Okay, how long before you automate my video editors?” There’s this [meme of my video editor editing the podcast](https://x.com/nkh1l/status/2022692208349188556?referrer=grok-com) every time I listen to this.

But the reason I do it is because I think it’s easy to get lost in abstractions when you talk about jobs you don’t understand well, and to very concretely understand what it takes to automate a job that I actually understand why it’s difficult for LLMs to currently take control over.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

I do think that the milestone for automating your video editor is earlier than the milestone of being able to automate all human jobs, including Texas politics, spinning up on the job. I do think that the video editor automation occurs maybe more around full automation of AI R&D, but it’s very sensitive to how much people are really focusing on understanding video.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

我觉得这个论证有三个不同的部分，我想逐个评估。第一，AI 研发非常可验证。第二，如果你把 AI 研发自动化了，就能在一年内拿到四五年的进展。第三，从「AI 研发被自动化」那一刻起、按当前速度再跑四五年的 AI 进展，出来的东西是一个你基本能扔到任何你想象得到的岗位上直接干活的 AI。

你可以把它扔进 1940 年代的德州政坛，它在权谋上能赢过[林登·约翰逊](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson)。你可以把它扔进 [TSMC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TSMC)，它能学会把台积电的制程工程做得更好。它当然也是个更好的视频剪辑师……我的视频剪辑师非常优秀，但它就是——总体上，在它所处的任何一份工作上都比人类更强。

所以我想把这些子论证挨个评估一遍，它们合起来推出的结论是：在你预期大约 2030 年达成的那个基准之后不久，ASI 就会到来，对吧？

**Ryan Greenblatt**

我会说，我预期 AI 研发的完全自动化大概在 2031、2030 年前后。而达到「在岗位上打败所有人类」这个里程碑，我的中位预期大概在 2033 年。但如果我真看到 AI 完全自动化了 AI 研发，我预期后者大概会在一年之内到来。预测这么算下来的结果就是：两个中位数之间的差，比里程碑之间差值的中位数更大。反正，随它去吧。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

顺带一提，网上有个梗。每次我想问别人的时间线时，[比如我问 Dario](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/dario-amodei-2) 或者别人，我总是问：「行，那还要多久才能把我的视频剪辑师自动化掉？」于是就有了[我的视频剪辑师在剪这期播客](https://x.com/nkh1l/status/2022692208349188556?referrer=grok-com)那个梗，每次我听到都会想起来。

但我这么问是有原因的：谈论你不熟悉的工作时，人很容易迷失在抽象里。我想非常具体地弄清楚，自动化一份我真正了解的工作到底需要什么——我很清楚为什么 LLM 目前还接管不了它。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

我确实认为，「自动化你的视频剪辑师」这个里程碑，会早于「能自动化所有人类工作、包括现学现干德州政治」那个里程碑。我确实觉得视频剪辑的自动化大概更接近 AI 研发完全自动化的时点，但这非常取决于人们在理解视频这件事上到底投入了多少精力。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

Okay, so let’s start with the claim that AI R&D is very verifiable.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

There’s a few different parts of this. One of them is that we can train on a bunch of environments which are basically directly training the model to do some AI R&D task or some very close-by task. For example, we can have some environment where the model is training some AI on just eight [H100s](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/) or some small amount of compute, and that model could be the equivalent of GPT-2 medium or whatever, and then similar to NanoGPT medium runs — and in [RL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning), it’s tweaking and iterating on that.

We could do that for a bunch of different tasks. We could have it train [image classification models](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/computer-vision/top-pre-trained-models-for-image-classification/), [video generation models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text-to-video_model), [image generation models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text-to-image_model), all kinds of different ML training tasks. We could RL it on the task of training increasingly good models, and also doing things like, “Oh, here’s a particular direction you could pursue for an algorithm. Can you go and implement that?”

Basically, there’s this whole class of containerizable, verifiable, small-scale AI R&D tasks that we can aggressively RL the AIs on. Already companies are presumably doing some RL on these sorts of tasks, and you could just keep scaling that up, keep making more of these small-scale AI R&D tasks, and then the AIs could keep getting better at this. Implicitly, I’m claiming this will transfer to extremely load-bearing aspects of AI R&D. But maybe let’s stop there for a second and then get to that part.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

好，那我们从「AI 研发非常可验证」这个主张开始。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

这里面有几个不同的部分。其中之一是：我们可以在一堆环境上训练模型，这些环境基本就是直接训练模型去做某个 AI 研发任务，或者某个非常邻近的任务。举个例子，我们可以搞一个环境，让模型在区区八块 [H100](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/h100/) 或者少量算力上训练某个 AI，那个模型可能相当于 GPT-2 medium 之类的规模，类似 NanoGPT medium 的训练跑——然后在 [RL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reinforcement_learning) 里让它不断调整、迭代。

我们可以针对一堆不同任务这么干。可以让它训练[图像分类模型](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/computer-vision/top-pre-trained-models-for-image-classification/)、[视频生成模型](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text-to-video_model)、[图像生成模型](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text-to-image_model)，各种各样的 ML 训练任务。我们可以就「训练出越来越好的模型」这个任务对它做 RL，也可以让它做这类事：「喏，这是一个你可以尝试的算法方向。你能不能去把它实现出来？」

基本上，存在这么一整类可容器化、可验证、小规模的 AI 研发任务，我们可以在上面对 AI 做激进的 RL。各家公司现在多半已经在做这类任务的 RL 了，你只要持续放大规模、持续造更多这种小规模 AI 研发任务，AI 就能在这上面持续变强。我这里隐含地在主张：这会迁移到 AI 研发中极其吃重的承重环节上。不过我们先在这打住，稍后再谈那部分。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

So let’s talk through what this concretely looks like. You can imagine that we have GPT-7.5. We say, “GPT-7.5, we want to make you so good at AI R&D that you help us train GPT-9.” So now we want to train GPT-7.5, and we come up with a bunch of different environments.

As you mentioned, there’s already this repo that is the [descendant](https://github.com/kellerjordan/modded-nanogpt) of [Andrej Karpathy](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy)‘s [nanoGPT](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT) speedrun, where you just try to change everything about the model, from the [optimizer](https://ml-cheatsheet.readthedocs.io/en/latest/optimizers.html) to the [hyperparameters](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/hyperparameter-tuning) to the architecture, to get it to a fixed training loss as fast as possible. You could have other kinds of environments where you could say, “Hey, GPT-7.5, I want you to train a really good video game-playing model. I want you to train a model that actually improves as it plays the same video game again and again. So you learn how to maybe help the model get better at online learning. We don’t care how you figure this out. Maybe it’s some kind of crazy [neuralese](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/qehggwKRMEyWqvjZG/reflections-on-neuralese) or a vector memory. Or maybe it’s just better long-context stuff. We don’t care. Figure out how to do [online learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_machine_learning) research.”

Obviously, GPT-7.5 will already be a smart model, and in the same way the models currently are getting smarter, it’ll be better and better at coding. You can imagine 100 other environments like this which are incentivizing the ability to do AI R&D, like containerized versions of getting GPT-7.5 to develop [GPT-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPT-2)\-sized models, et cetera. Then you basically put GPT-7.5 through a bunch of this kind of training, you build GPT-8. GPT-8 is now an amazing ML researcher. It has so much intuition from doing all this kind of training.

Honestly, a huge intuition pump for me is seeing the [progress that AI has made in mathematics](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2583307-why-mathematician-terence-tao-thinks-ai-must-spark-a-rapid-revolution/). If it’s a very verifiable domain, AIs can get… I don’t really know the object-level details of mathematics research, but I’m just like, “No, it works.” It can just come in like a flood if you can totally put it into a verification loop, and it can actually make new breakthroughs.

I am curious if ML research has a quality of mathematical research where it seems like there was a big overhang from connecting different disciplines together. No one person would have known enough about algebraic geometry and… What was the right word?
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

那我们把这个具体是什么样子过一遍。你可以设想我们有 GPT-7.5。我们说：「GPT-7.5，我们要让你在 AI 研发上牛到能帮我们训练出 GPT-9。」于是现在我们要训练 GPT-7.5，我们造出一堆不同的环境。

你刚提到，现在已经有这么一个仓库，是 [Andrej Karpathy](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/andrej-karpathy) 的 [nanoGPT](https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT) speedrun 的[后裔](https://github.com/kellerjordan/modded-nanogpt)：你把模型的一切都改一遍，从[优化器](https://ml-cheatsheet.readthedocs.io/en/latest/optimizers.html)到[超参](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/hyperparameter-tuning)到架构，目标是尽可能快地打到某个固定的训练 loss。你还可以有别的环境，比如说：「嘿 GPT-7.5，我要你训练一个特别能玩电子游戏的模型。我要一个反复玩同一个游戏、真的会越玩越强的模型。所以你得搞明白怎么帮模型把在线学习做好。我们不管你怎么搞出来的。可能是某种疯狂的 [neuralese](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/qehggwKRMEyWqvjZG/reflections-on-neuralese)，或者向量记忆。也可能就是更好的长上下文机制。我们不在乎。你自己去把[在线学习](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Online_machine_learning)研究搞定。」

显然，GPT-7.5 本身已经是个聪明模型了，而且就像当下模型正在变聪明那样，它写代码会越来越强。你可以设想还有 100 个类似的环境，全都在激励 AI 研发能力，比如把「让 GPT-7.5 去开发 [GPT-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPT-2) 规模的模型」容器化，诸如此类。然后你基本上就是让 GPT-7.5 走一遍这类训练，造出 GPT-8。GPT-8 现在是个了不起的 ML 研究员了，它从这一整套训练里攒下了大量直觉。

老实说，对我而言一个巨大的直觉泵是看到 [AI 在数学上取得的进展](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2583307-why-mathematician-terence-tao-thinks-ai-must-spark-a-rapid-revolution/)。如果一个领域非常可验证，AI 就能……我并不真的了解数学研究的对象层细节，但我的感受就是：「不用问，它就是行。」只要你能把它整个塞进一个验证回路，它就能像洪水一样涌进来，而且真能做出新突破。

我很好奇：ML 研究是否具备数学研究的那种特质——看起来打通不同学科之间的连接本身就存在巨大的悬垂（overhang）。没有任何一个人能同时懂足够多的代数几何和……那个词该怎么说来着？

bilingual.en:
**Ryan Greenblatt**

Oh man, I really don’t know about the math breakthroughs.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

No one person would’ve known enough about [topology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology) and algebraic whatever in order to make [some counterexample to a big conjecture](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/ai-disproves-a-decades-old-mathematical-idea-the-biggest-conjecture-that-the-tech-has-played-a-role-in-yet-180989189/).

**Ryan Greenblatt**

My view is that ML is a less deep domain than math, and so there’s less of a thing where there are individual experts with really deep expertise in some area that they combine, but there’s definitely going to be some of that.

But then I also think that ML has some attributes that make it even more favorable to AI training than mathematics in some ways. In particular, you can get a better sense of whether you’re succeeding, and you can see intermediate progress. In math, it’s often the case that there’s no easy way to see whether or not you’re close to success. Whereas if your goal is, for example, to get to some training loss 2x faster, you can kind of see when you’re halfway there. It tends to be the case that ML innovations are very additive, or maybe multiplicative depending on how you think about it, where basically you can keep stacking innovations. Usually the innovations just add together and don’t interfere with each other, though obviously it’s going to depend on the details.

So I think that in a lot of ways, AI R&D will have properties quite similar to math, where you can train on chunks of AI R&D that are pretty similar in structure to the problem you actually cared about, in a very verifiable way, and then that will transfer. There’s an open question of exactly how well it will transfer, but I think that the transfer currently for math looks pretty good. My expectation is that the transfer for AI R&D will look pretty good, but not amazing.
bilingual.zh:
**Ryan Greenblatt**

天哪，数学突破那块我是真不懂。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

没有任何一个人能同时懂足够多的[拓扑学](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topology)和代数什么什么，从而[给某个大猜想造出反例](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/ai-disproves-a-decades-old-mathematical-idea-the-biggest-conjecture-that-the-tech-has-played-a-role-in-yet-180989189/)。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

我的看法是，ML 是个比数学浅的领域，所以那种「有若干专家各自在某个领域有极深的造诣、再把它们组合起来」的成分会更少，但肯定还是会有一些。

不过我也认为，ML 有些属性使它在某些方面比数学更适合用来训练 AI。特别是，你能更清楚地判断自己是不是在成功，你能看见中间进展。在数学里，往往没有简单办法判断你离成功还有多远。而如果你的目标是——比如说——把达到某个训练 loss 的速度提升 2 倍，你多少能看出自己是不是走到一半了。ML 的创新往往是可加的，或者说取决于你怎么看是可乘的——基本上你可以不断把创新叠上去，通常这些创新就是相加、互不干扰，当然这显然要看具体细节。

所以我认为在很多方面，AI 研发会有跟数学相当类似的性质：你可以在结构上跟你真正关心的问题很相似的 AI 研发片段上训练，而且是以非常可验证的方式，然后它会迁移过去。至于迁移得到底有多好是个开放问题，但我认为数学目前的迁移效果看上去相当不错。我的预期是 AI 研发的迁移效果也会相当不错，但称不上惊艳。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

So one concern I have is that I think even in mathematics, as far as I’m aware, we have not seen very impressive new theory. We’ve seen a lot of impressive, verifiable, specific results — for example, find a counterexample to this conjecture — but we have not seen “come up with the idea of [topology](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Topology.html)“ kinds of levels of things, or “come up with things like [group theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory)“.

It seems like ML research has elements of both of these things. But the less verifiable thing of coming up with new ways of thinking about the problem would be harder to induce. Take, for example, the idea of [scaling laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_scaling_law). Obviously, there is some end verification loop such that you can train GPT-4 better if you have the [idea of scaling laws from 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361). But there is a longer and potentially more compute-laden road to inducing AIs to be like, “Okay, I got to think carefully about how I should be scaling my parameters and data. What are different kinds of investigations I could run to understand this? Maybe I can come up with a visualization and an [isoFLOP analysis](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/isoflops-analysis) or something.” But that does seem like a longer verification loop than just, “Hey, let’s get nanoGPT loss to go down.”

**Ryan Greenblatt**

Let’s talk about this. First of all, I think in the context of math, the thing I would say is that the AIs can do the equivalent of ‘baby’s first new theory,’ where, for example, they can just prove interesting conjectures via making connections and producing new understanding. It’s like, “Oh, there’s this construction the AI found which is pretty interesting”, or it found this way of thinking about the problem that’s a bit different. We do see that. It’s just that the examples we see are not as impressive as founding the field of group theory.

Founding the field of group theory is probably among the best, biggest mathematical accomplishments of all time, and the AIs just aren’t that good at math yet. From my perspective, there’s a continuum between that and the things we’re seeing now, that the AIs are continuing to march up.

Second, I think ML is a very shallow domain relative to math. In math, there was much more of a thing where you find some true deep abstraction, and if you really understand that thing, which is hard to understand, then you get somewhere. Whereas I feel like the things that are the equivalent of that in ML are really dumb bullshit. Like with scaling laws, come on guys, we can explain scaling laws really quickly. I think the deepest and most important concepts in math, for example, don’t have the property that you can really understand the underlying thing and why it matters in a very short period of time.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

我的一个顾虑是：据我所知，即便在数学里，我们也还没见到非常惊艳的新理论。我们见到了大量惊艳的、可验证的具体结果——比如给某个猜想找反例——但我们没见到「想出[拓扑学](https://mathworld.wolfram.com/Topology.html)这个东西」这种级别，或者「想出[群论](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_theory)这种东西」。

ML 研究看起来两种成分都有。但「想出思考问题的新方式」这种不那么可验证的部分，会更难被诱导出来。拿[缩放定律](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neural_scaling_law)（scaling laws）举例。显然，末端是有验证回路的——如果你有 [2020 年那个缩放定律的想法](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361)，你就能把 GPT-4 训得更好。但要诱导出 AI 说出「好，我得仔细想想参数和数据该怎么缩放。我可以跑哪些不同的调查来搞懂这件事？也许我能做个可视化，来个 [isoFLOP 分析](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/isoflops-analysis)之类的」，这条路更长、也可能更吃算力。这看上去确实是个比「嘿，把 nanoGPT 的 loss 打下去」长得多的验证回路。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

来聊聊这个。首先，在数学的语境下，我想说的是：AI 能做出相当于「婴儿的第一个新理论」的东西——比如它们能通过建立连接、产生新理解来证明有意思的猜想。就是那种「哦，AI 找到了这么一个构造，挺有意思的」，或者它找到了某种略微不同的思考问题的方式。这我们是看得到的。只不过我们看到的例子还没有开创群论那么惊艳。

开创群论大概是有史以来最了不起、最重大的数学成就之一，而 AI 的数学还没好到那份上。在我看来，从那个高度到我们现在看到的东西之间是个连续谱，而 AI 正在这个谱上持续向上爬。

第二，我认为相对于数学，ML 是个非常浅的领域。数学里更多存在这种情形：你找到某个真正深刻的抽象，那东西很难理解，但只要你真懂了它，你就能到达某个地方。而我感觉 ML 里对应的那些东西，其实都是些挺蠢的破玩意儿。就拿缩放定律来说，拜托各位，缩放定律我们几句话就能讲明白。而我认为数学里最深刻、最重要的那些概念，并不具备「你能在很短时间内真正理解底层的东西以及它为什么重要」这种性质。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

But I feel like one effect will be that we will have gotten rid of all the low-hanging fruits by 2030. I feel like scaling laws will have been, in math history, like [Descartes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Descartes) finding the [Cartesian grid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_coordinate_system) and doing very basic mathematics. Eventually, if we want to keep making progress in the 2030s, it’s going to be like doing whatever bullshit is happening at the frontiers of mathematics right now.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

That could be right. My sense is that some domains are structurally different in terms of how they operate and how much they depend on deep abstractions. Physics and math are much more on the side of being very far on the deep, hard-to-come-up-with-ideas side, whereas I think ML and most other domains are much more amenable to [hill climbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_climbing). That’s my sense of how this will go in the future.

Even in the regime where your AIs are having to plow — it’s 2030, a bunch of low-hanging fruit in research has already happened, and they need to make further progress — I still suspect that a bunch of the work will live more on the side of building increasingly complicated infrastructure and having really good intuition about what the experiments roughly look like. So I’m probably less sympathetic to the idea that the thing the AIs will lack is some deep insight. I’m more sympathetic to the idea that they really need a bunch of taste about in-the-weeds experiments that they currently don’t have. They need a bunch of intuition for what sorts of training approaches would work and what wouldn’t, in ways that current researchers have.

Even in cases where there has been some breakthrough in AI, oftentimes in retrospect it looks like a big bottleneck to making that breakthrough happen was getting all of the micro details and mungy intuition right. An example of this is training AIs to be good at reasoning and [chain of thought](https://research.google/blog/language-models-perform-reasoning-via-chain-of-thought/), doing RL on chain of thought. It looks like you probably could have done RL and chain of thought on GPT-3 and gotten kind of interesting results on math if you had really scaled it up and done a good job.

But at the time, there was low-hanging fruit. Also, doing a good job with that training is kind of in the weeds on all the technical implementation and scaling it up and getting the hyperparameters right. So maybe you can demonstrate everything on [Qwen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qwen) [1B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen1.5-1.8B) or whatever and get some sense that this whole thing is going to work. But people didn’t demonstrate it as early as they could have because of all of these other mungy details and intuition about exactly how to tune the parameters and how to set things up.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

但我觉得会有这么一个效应：到 2030 年，我们已经把所有低垂果实摘光了。我感觉在数学史上，缩放定律相当于[笛卡尔](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Descartes)发明[笛卡尔坐标系](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_coordinate_system)、在做非常基础的数学。到最后，如果我们想在 2030 年代继续推进，那就得去做当下数学前沿正在搞的那些鬼名堂。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

有可能。我的感觉是，不同领域在运作方式上、在多大程度上依赖深层抽象上，是有结构性差别的。物理和数学远远偏向「深、想法极难被想出来」那一侧，而我认为 ML 和大多数其他领域，则更适合[爬山法](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_climbing)（hill climbing）。这就是我对未来走向的判断。

即便进入那种你的 AI 不得不硬啃的阶段——时间到了 2030 年，研究里一大堆低垂果实已经被摘掉了，它们得继续往前推——我仍然怀疑，大部分工作会更偏向于搭建越来越复杂的基础设施，以及对实验大致长什么样有非常好的直觉。所以我大概不太认同「AI 会缺的是某种深刻洞见」这个说法。我更认同的是：它们真正需要的是一大堆当下还不具备的、关于泥地里实验细节的品味（taste）。它们需要一堆关于哪些训练路子能work、哪些不行的直觉——那是现在的研究员身上有的东西。

即便是那些 AI 领域确实发生过突破的案例，事后回看也常常会发现，突破之所以能发生，一个大瓶颈是把所有微观细节和脏活直觉搞对了。一个例子就是训练 AI 擅长推理和[思维链](https://research.google/blog/language-models-perform-reasoning-via-chain-of-thought/)（chain of thought），也就是在思维链上做 RL。看起来你当年在 GPT-3 上做思维链 RL 大概也能work，只要你真把规模放上去、把活干好，就能在数学上拿到还挺有意思的结果。

但在当时，还有低垂果实可摘。而且把那套训练做好，很大程度上是在泥地里跟各种技术实现细节、扩规模、把超参调对这些事情较劲。所以也许你可以在 [Qwen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qwen) [1B](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen1.5-1.8B) 之类的模型上把整套东西演示一遍，大致确认这条路走得通。但人们没能在本可以更早的时候把它演示出来，就是因为所有这些琐碎脏细节，以及到底该怎么调参数、怎么把整套东西搭起来的直觉。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

This is my remaining skepticism, honestly, about this story. I’m not sure I understand why, if research breakthroughs are so amenable to intelligence, AI progress has not been historically faster than it could have been. As you were saying, by the time [RLVR](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/rl-with-verifiable-rewards-rlvr) actually worked — even though you could have done it with less compute — we had to wait for oceans of compute, gigawatts of compute, to be available before people were doing this training, on the trajectory of compute continuing to increase so we make more breakthroughs.

I don’t know. I feel like there were a lot of AI researchers in the year 2022 who were trying to crack reasoning. Was it just that they were bottlenecked by the ability to write infrastructure code, or what was happening?

**Ryan Greenblatt**

It’s a complicated mix. I think they would have gone faster if they could, as soon as they thought of an experiment, run that experiment without bugs, without bugs being very important. And then another part of it is that being able to run a lot of experiments at high compute lets you paper over ways in which the way you implemented it isn’t quite right or you didn’t have the right hyperparameters. So compute is just really helpful for doing AI research, and you can cover over a lot of things. But that doesn’t mean that massive increases in labor wouldn’t also be helpful, especially if that labor comes with among the best intuitions that people have in the field. I just think that’s really helpful.

Another part of my perspective here, which is maybe a bit different from where you’re coming from, is that I’m expecting somewhat more transfer than you seem to be imagining. I’m imagining these AIs are actually pretty good scientists in general and are pretty reasonable at all of that stuff. When you interact with them, it’s not like they have some really hyper-specialized savant-type vibe. They’re actually pretty good at all of the stuff in R&D, and then maybe extremely good at some subdomains. So they’re incredibly superhuman at writing [kernels](https://modal.com/gpu-glossary/device-software/kernel), incredibly superhuman at everything with very short feedback loops, and then pretty good at all the other stuff, totally able to match other people.

I think we are seeing this now. When I look at AIs right now, it’s already the case that they can pretty competently match humans who are mediocre at ML research at doing ML research. It’s just that being mediocre at ML research is not that helpful. The thing you actually want are people who are good at ML research. My sense is the AIs are just improving at all of these things. Their taste is improving, their intuition is improving, and it’s already the case that their taste and intuition is not complete garbage.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

老实说，这是我对这套叙事残留的怀疑所在。我不太明白：如果研究突破真这么吃智能，为什么 AI 的历史进展没有比实际更快？就像你说的，等到 [RLVR](https://www.emergentmind.com/topics/rl-with-verifiable-rewards-rlvr) 真正跑通的时候——哪怕你本可以用更少的算力做出来——我们还是得等到算力如汪洋、以吉瓦计地铺开，人们才开始做这种训练，走在一条「算力持续增长、于是我们做出更多突破」的轨迹上。

我不知道。我感觉 2022 年有一大堆 AI 研究员在试图攻克推理。难道当时他们的瓶颈就是写基础设施代码的能力吗？还是说发生了别的什么？

**Ryan Greenblatt**

这是个复杂的混合体。我认为，如果他们能做到「一想到某个实验就马上跑起来、而且没有 bug」，他们会走得更快——没有 bug 这点非常重要。另一部分是：能在高算力下跑大量实验，可以帮你把实现得不太对、或者超参没调对的地方糊过去。所以算力对做 AI 研究真的很有用，能掩盖掉很多问题。但这不代表劳动力的大幅增加就不管用，尤其当这些劳动力还自带业内最好的直觉时。我认为那真的非常有用。

我这边还有另一个视角，可能跟你的出发点有点不同：我预期的迁移程度比你设想的更高。我设想的是，这些 AI 其实是相当不错的通用科学家，在所有这些事情上都挺靠谱。你跟它们打交道时，不会觉得它们有那种高度专精的学者症候群式气质。它们在研发的各个环节上都相当在行，然后在某些子领域可能极其在行。所以它们写[内核](https://modal.com/gpu-glossary/device-software/kernel)（kernel）时是极端超人的，在一切反馈回路很短的事情上都是极端超人的，然后在其他所有事情上也相当不错，完全能跟其他人打平。

我认为我们现在已经看到这一点了。我现在看这些 AI，它们已经能相当胜任地在 ML 研究上跟那些「ML 研究做得平庸」的人打平了。问题只是，ML 研究做得平庸并没什么大用。你真正想要的是 ML 研究做得好的人。我的感觉是 AI 在所有这些方面都在进步。它们的品味在提升，直觉在提升，而且它们的品味和直觉现在已经不是彻头彻尾的垃圾了。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

I want to very concretely understand what it would look like for five years of AI progress to happen in one year. Suppose we were back when GPT-3 was developed. The idea is that, with the level of compute they had back in 2022, if we had automated AI R&D back then, you could at the end of that year have Mythos.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

That would be the idea, yes.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

[Mythos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Mythos) took way more compute than they had back then, but even with the level of compute they had back then, not only do all the breakthroughs happen, but they also train Mythos with that level of compute.

What would be required is obviously discovering all the algorithmic progress since then. It’s discovering even more, actually, because you’ve got to make up for the fact that Mythos uses… What was GPT-3 trained on? Like 1e23? We can look it up. But is it plausibly four orders of magnitude more compute?

**Ryan Greenblatt**

I think it’s somewhat less than that. Let’s look this up quickly. GPT-3 training compute is about 3e23. My sense is that Mythos is probably a little over three [OOMs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_magnitude) higher. So the question is: can you overcome this 1000x compute gap while also being the model?

Here’s a concrete claim that maybe we should talk about. Right now, would we be able to train a model with GPT-3-level compute that matches… What exactly do I think? GPT-3 was released in 2020, so it was trained about six and a half, seven years ago. It’s worth noting that GPT-3 is maybe a little too far in the past, but let’s go with this for a second.

If we were to train a model with GPT-3-level compute today, how good would that model be? My understanding, based on how algorithmic progress works, is that we’d be able to train a model that’s as good as the best model we had perhaps around three years ago. So I think that right now we’d be able to train a version of GPT-3 that’s probably somewhat better than GPT-4, a moderate amount better than GPT-4. I think that’s about right. That roughly lines up with how algorithmic progress has worked.

Basically, the story would end up being that to get five years of AI progress, you’re probably going to need around, I would say, maybe eight years of algorithmic progress, very roughly, which is a lot of algorithmic progress. But it just turns out that most of the AI progress, from my perspective, has come from some mix of algorithms and data, and you can just keep making huge improvements on these things and training AIs with less compute.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

我想非常具体地弄清楚，「一年内发生五年的 AI 进展」到底长什么样。假设我们回到 GPT-3 被开发出来的时候。这个想法是说：以他们 2022 年手头的算力水平，如果我们当时就把 AI 研发自动化了，那一年结束时你就能拿到 Mythos。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

对，就是这个意思。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

[Mythos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Mythos) 用掉的算力远远超过他们当时所有的，但即便只用当时那个算力水平，不仅所有突破都要发生，他们还得用那个算力水平把 Mythos 训出来。

要做到这点，显然得把此后所有的算法进展全部发现出来。实际上还得发现更多，因为你得补上 Mythos 用了……GPT-3 是用多少算力训的来着？1e23 左右？我们可以查一下。但差距有可能是四个数量级吗？

**Ryan Greenblatt**

我认为比这少一些。我们快速查一下。GPT-3 的训练算力大约是 3e23。我的感觉是 Mythos 大概比它高三个[数量级](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_magnitude)（OOM）出头。所以问题是：你能不能在自己就是那个模型的同时，把这 1000 倍的算力差距克服掉？

这里有个具体的主张，也许我们可以聊聊。现在，我们有没有可能用 GPT-3 级别的算力训出一个模型，达到……我到底怎么想的来着？GPT-3 是 2020 年发布的，所以它大约是六年半、七年前训的。值得说明的是，GPT-3 可能有点太久远了，但我们先就这么算。

如果我们今天用 GPT-3 级别的算力训一个模型，那模型会有多好？按我对算法进展如何运作的理解，我们大概能训出一个跟三年前最好的模型一样好的模型。所以我认为现在我们能训出的那个「GPT-3 版本」，大概会比 GPT-4 好一些，比 GPT-4 好上中等幅度。我觉得这个判断大致没错，跟算法进展的历史规律大体对得上。

基本上，故事会变成这样：要拿到五年的 AI 进展，你大概需要——我会说——粗略估计八年左右的算法进展，那是非常大量的算法进展。但事实就是，在我看来 AI 进展的绝大部分来自算法和数据的某种混合，而你可以在这些东西上持续做出巨大改进，用更少的算力训出 AI。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

I’m glad you brought that up, because what has happened since GPT-3, or even 3.5, till now? Why is Mythos so good? Obviously, we’ve scaled the compute. We have better algorithms. But a huge thing that’s happened is that we have built a deca-billion-dollar data industry which has systematically collected and codified expert human judgment across all kinds of different disciplines — codified in the form of RL environments, codified in the form of [SFT](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/artificial-intelligence/supervised-fine-tuning-sft-for-llms/) traces — that these experts built to help the model better understand how you do coding, how you build complex infrastructure projects, how you do law, how you do whatever. How are the AIs able to replicate the effect that expert human judgment currently seems to be playing in AI progress?

**Ryan Greenblatt**

My sense is that scaling up the amount of effort spent on getting expert human data has not been hugely important for AI R&D in general. In particular, over the last few years, we’ve been scaling up compute, scaling up people working at AI companies, and scaling up the amount of effort spent on data labeling. My sense is that if you removed the last two doublings or whatever of data generation from expert humans, that would not make a huge difference. A lot of what’s been going on is people have been developing better ways to leverage humans and AIs to construct RL environments and going somewhere from that.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

But how do you explain why the AIs have gotten so good at coding? I feel like a big part of that is data and RL environments, which are codifying human experts.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

But the question is what is the limiting factor on creating RL environments? My sense is that the reason why RL environments today are much better than they were in 2024 is not so much because we have hired way more human experts to make RL environments. It is instead much more because we better know what RL environments we even want to make and how we should structure them. Also, we’re using huge amounts of AI labor to build RL environments. I think those effects are much more important than the effect of human labor building the RL environments.

I’m not saying that the human labor doesn’t matter. I’m just saying there are other big drivers that are important here. I could try to argue for this. One thing is just that the amount of environments people want is a very large amount. I think the AIs are actually pretty good at the task of making RL environments given some sense of what the thing should be. There’s preexisting data you could use. A lot of these things have good verification loops.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

很高兴你提到这个，因为从 GPT-3、甚至 3.5 到现在，究竟发生了什么？为什么 Mythos 这么好？显然，我们扩了算力，我们有了更好的算法。但另一件大事是：我们建起了一个百亿美元级的数据产业，它系统性地收集并编码了各行各业的人类专家判断——编码成 RL 环境，编码成 [SFT](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/artificial-intelligence/supervised-fine-tuning-sft-for-llms/) 轨迹——这些都是那些专家造出来的，用来帮模型更好地理解怎么写代码、怎么做复杂的基础设施项目、怎么做法律、怎么做别的什么。AI 要如何复制专家人类判断当下在 AI 进展中扮演的这个作用？

**Ryan Greenblatt**

我的感觉是，把「获取专家人类数据」上投入的精力扩大规模，对 AI 研发整体而言并没有多么重要。特别是，过去这几年我们一直在扩算力、扩 AI 公司的人手、扩数据标注上投入的精力。我的感觉是，如果你把最近这两个翻倍的专家人类数据生成量拿掉，那不会造成多大差别。真正在发生的很大一部分，是人们开发出了更好的方式去调动人和 AI 来构建 RL 环境，并由此往前走。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

但你怎么解释 AI 在写代码上变得这么强？我觉得很大一部分就是数据和 RL 环境，而它们正是在编码人类专家。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

但问题是，创建 RL 环境的限制因素是什么？我的感觉是，今天的 RL 环境比 2024 年好得多，主要原因并不是我们雇了多得多的人类专家来造 RL 环境，而更多是因为我们更清楚自己到底想造什么样的 RL 环境、该怎么组织它们。而且我们在用海量的 AI 劳动力来构建 RL 环境。我认为这些效应比人类劳动力造 RL 环境这件事重要得多。

我不是说人类劳动力不重要，我只是说这里还有其他重要的大驱动力。这一点我可以试着论证。一个理由是，人们想要的环境数量非常庞大。我认为，只要给 AI 一个「这东西大致该是什么样」的概念，它们其实相当擅长造 RL 环境这件事。有现成的数据可以用。这些东西里很多都有不错的验证回路。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

Just look at, for example, what was reported in _Business Insider_ yesterday, that [Google is paying close to $2 billion for Mechanize](https://www.businessinsider.com/google-mechanize-deal-talent-tech-ai-coding-2026-8). We can just look at market rates for what people think really good human expert data is worth. The frontier labs seem to think it’s worth a lot. They’re willing to pay for it.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

What fraction of frontier lab spending do you think is on data rather than compute? What do you think is the compute/data spend split?

**Dwarkesh Patel**

I think it’s overwhelmingly compute, but I also think it’s because compute is easier to scale up than data.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

But that’s really relevant to what’s driving progress, right? My sense is that the split is something like 20 to 1 or 10 to 1. I don’t know exactly. It depends on the company.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

But this is similar to how oil is 1.5% of GDP. That doesn’t mean that if you cut oil out, GDP could continue to run.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

Sure, but it contradicts your argument, right?

**Dwarkesh Patel**

The economy would come to a halt immediately if oil went away.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

Sure, but you were just arguing that because of the high market cap, we can learn that this is the key driver, and I’m saying that’s not clearly true. That argument just makes it look like compute is a much more important driver, or hiring employees is a much more important driver.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

看看昨天《_Business Insider_》报道的那件事：[Google 出价接近 20 亿美元收购 Mechanize](https://www.businessinsider.com/google-mechanize-deal-talent-tech-ai-coding-2026-8)。我们可以直接看市场价——人们认为真正优质的人类专家数据值多少钱。前沿实验室看起来认为它值很多钱，他们愿意为此掏钱。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

你觉得前沿实验室的开支里，花在数据而非算力上的比例是多少？你认为算力和数据的开支比是多少？

**Dwarkesh Patel**

我认为压倒性地是算力，但我也认为那是因为算力比数据更容易扩规模。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

但这跟「什么在驱动进展」这个问题高度相关，对吧？我的感觉是这个比例大概是 20 比 1 或者 10 比 1。我不知道确切数字，这取决于是哪家公司。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

但这就好比石油只占 GDP 的 1.5%。这不代表你把石油抽走，GDP 还能继续运转。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

当然，但这跟你自己的论证矛盾了，对吧？

**Dwarkesh Patel**

石油一没，经济立刻就停摆了。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

当然，可你刚才的论证是：因为市值高，所以我们能推断这是关键驱动力——而我要说的是，这个推断并不明显成立。那个论证反倒会让人觉得算力是重要得多的驱动力，或者雇员工是重要得多的驱动力。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

So maybe let’s be more concrete. Here’s what I think. My claim is that if you went back to 2022 and you had GPT-3.5, and you were trying to make it better at coding without human experts, I think it would have just been very, very difficult.

Let me give you an example of what I imagine would be the difficulty of going from GPT-8 to [ASI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintelligence). One of the things you’d want ASI to be good at is: I’m going to take over a company and make it much more profitable and do all kinds of crazy shit to make it work better. I’m going to take over a fab and produce more chips. I’m going to go into Congress and try to convince them to pass some bill, et cetera.

This is what I imagine five more years of AI progress at this pace would enable an AI to be able to do. This is the thing I’m really worried about: ASI that can understand how to do crazy shit in the world, that can do what [Kissinger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kissinger) can do, can do what Steve Jobs can do, et cetera, and also his engineers and so on. I’m not sure how you get that without the relevant world data, which is the equivalent of Mythos being really good at coding while not having the coding environments that have improved it relative to GPT-3.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

Here are a few points. First, I bet if you look at randomly sampled training environments for Mythos, they’re actually very different from what it looks like to actually use the model in practice. My sense is that the RL distribution has really large deviations from the real-world data distribution, and it’s significantly smoothed over by a mix of transfer and having a small amount of data focused on the real world. My sense is that this will be a similar mechanism as how it works for the crazy, wildly, quite superhuman AI you get as a result of five years of AI progress on top of fully automated AI R&D.

So let’s go through this a little bit. In particular, I think that you could train an AI to be really, really good at learning on the fly and doing something analogous to [in-context learning](https://intro-to-icl.github.io/), but potentially using somewhat different mechanisms, in a wide variety of RL environments. You build all these different RL environments where the AI has to adapt on the fly, learn on the fly, figure out what it should do, understand its situation better, and learn really quickly from feedback in order to succeed at its objective. And it has things like limited resources, and if it messes up, it can end up in a much worse position.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

那我们说得更具体点。我是这么想的。我的主张是：如果你回到 2022 年，手里拿着 GPT-3.5，试图在没有人类专家的情况下让它更擅长写代码，我认为那会非常非常困难。

我给你举个例子，说明我设想中从 GPT-8 走到 [ASI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superintelligence) 的难点在哪。你希望 ASI 擅长的事情之一是：我要接管一家公司，把它的利润率大幅提上去，为了让它运转得更好什么疯狂的事都干。我要接管一座晶圆厂，多产芯片。我要走进国会，试图说服他们通过某项法案，等等。

这就是我设想中「以当前速度再走五年 AI 进展」会让 AI 能做到的事。这也是我真正担心的东西：一个懂得如何在现实世界里搞出疯狂操作的 ASI，能做[基辛格](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Kissinger)能做的事，能做史蒂夫·乔布斯能做的事，等等，还能干他手下工程师的活。我不太明白，在没有相关的世界数据的情况下你怎么拿到这个能力——这就相当于说，Mythos 在没有那些让它相对 GPT-3 突飞猛进的编程环境的情况下，还能变得非常擅长写代码。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

我有几点。第一，我打赌如果你去随机抽样 Mythos 的训练环境，它们其实跟人们实际使用这个模型时的样子非常不同。我的感觉是，RL 分布跟真实世界的数据分布有非常大的偏离，而这个偏离被「迁移」加上「少量聚焦真实世界的数据」这套混合机制大幅抹平了。我的感觉是，对于那个「在完全自动化的 AI 研发之上再跑五年 AI 进展」所产出的、疯狂到远超人类的 AI，机制也会是类似的。

那我们把这个稍微过一遍。特别是，我认为你可以训练一个 AI 变得非常非常擅长即时学习（learning on the fly），做某种类似[上下文学习](https://intro-to-icl.github.io/)（in-context learning）的事情——但可能用的是有所不同的机制——而且是在种类繁多的 RL 环境里训。你搭出各种各样的环境，AI 必须在其中即时适应、即时学习、想清楚自己该做什么、更好地理解自身处境、并从反馈中飞快学习，才能达成目标。而且它面对的还有资源有限这类约束，一旦搞砸，处境会糟糕得多。

bilingual.en:
If you train on a huge number of these environments, you will learn general skills of picking up context on the fly, and we’re already seeing this. It’s already the case that AIs are now much better at understanding roughly what’s going on and picking up context from a limited amount of information they’re given access to.

Then those AIs could be put on the job at TSMC. Even though TSMC is not literally in their data distribution, their data distribution is really wide, and the AIs are extremely good on their data distribution, such that it transfers to picking up being good at being an engineer at TSMC and learning that on the fly. The way the AI gets good at being a TSMC engineer isn’t that it has a ton of cached knowledge on being a good TSMC engineer. It’s that it does the equivalent of some scaled-up version of in-context learning there.

That’d be the most prosaic story. Obviously, there’s a bunch of different ways this could go.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

I think this maybe comes down to a difference of intuition about how far you can get. When I think about really smart people I know, they’re just not that effective in domains they don’t understand that well.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

But how long have they had to learn?

**Dwarkesh Patel**

I agree that if they had experience, they would be much better. But that’s maybe what I’m arguing for, that experience with data. For example, if I just get a really smart Ivy League college grad, and I’m like, “Okay, you’re now in charge of negotiating the Iran deal,” I think they just wouldn’t know what to do.
bilingual.zh:
如果你在海量这类环境上训练，模型就会学到「即时获取上下文」的通用技能，而且这一点我们已经看到了。现在的 AI 在「大致搞清楚状况是什么」以及「从有限的可获取信息里捞出上下文」这两件事上，已经强了很多。

然后你就可以把这些 AI 放到台积电（TSMC）的岗位上。哪怕台积电并不真的在它们的数据分布里，但它们的数据分布非常宽，而 AI 在自己的数据分布上又极其强，强到足以迁移出「胜任一名台积电工程师」并且现学现用。AI 变得擅长做台积电工程师，靠的不是它缓存了一大堆「怎么当好台积电工程师」的知识，而是它在那里做了某种放大版的 in-context learning（上下文内学习）。

这会是最平淡无奇的那个版本的故事。当然，事情还有一堆别的走法。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

我觉得这里的分歧，可能归结为对「你能走多远」的直觉不同。我想到我认识的那些真正聪明的人，他们在自己不太懂的领域里，其实并没有那么高效。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

但他们有多长时间去学？

**Dwarkesh Patel**

我同意，如果他们有经验，会强得多。但这大概正是我要论证的东西——用数据换来的那种经验。比如说，我随便找一个非常聪明的常春藤应届毕业生，跟他说：「好，现在伊朗核协议的谈判归你负责了」，我觉得他会完全不知道该干什么。

bilingual.en:
**Ryan Greenblatt**

I think if you instead got someone who is really good at quickly picking up a bunch of different domains and you gave them some time to train and talk to people and shore up their expertise and do some practice, they would actually do a pretty good job. I think most domains are fundamentally pretty shallow, where a very smart generalist who’s good at a limited subset of core skills can get going pretty quickly. That’s not true for literally every domain. My sense is that the AIs will develop increasingly good mechanisms for quickly acquiring understanding and expertise in a given domain.

Consider, for example, how fast AIs can understand a new code base. AIs can understand a new code base much faster than humans can, but to a degree that’s shallower than humans could currently understand. But it’s getting better over time. Let me spell that argument out a bit more. Let’s say you take Fable 5 or Mythos 5 or whatever, and you wanted to make some kind of complicated change to a really massive code base. The model will get some understanding of the code base very fast, in the course of maybe significantly less than an hour, potentially much less than an hour. Then its understanding of the code base will plateau a little bit, where it won’t get as deep of an understanding as a human would have gotten over a much longer period.

So it’s like an AI in an hour can match a human with a few weeks maybe, depending on the details of exactly how complicated the code base is. But it won’t match a human who’s been working on that code base for two years or whatever. But over time, the amount of understanding AIs can match has gone up. If we look at [3.7 Sonnet](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-3-7-sonnet) or [3.5 Sonnet](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-3-5-sonnet), maybe it could only match the equivalent of understanding a code base for a day or something.

But now AIs are much better at building context about a task. So you can be like, “Mythos, I want you to really understand this code base, and then implement this feature.” It will spawn a bajillion sub-agents. Those sub-agents will pore over a bunch of things. It will deliver a bunch of context back. It will then investigate a few things. It’s not amazing at doing this, but it can happen really fast, and it can work pretty well.

And it’s not very hard for me to imagine how you could train AIs to be increasingly good at this task. The task of implementing some very complicated feature in some reasonable way in a very big code base is extremely verifiable, and that can be a thing the AIs improve on. Similarly, there’s a broader skill of quickly understanding context and being able to have a bunch of different AIs learn in parallel and then merging that together.
bilingual.zh:
**Ryan Greenblatt**

我觉得，如果你换成一个非常擅长快速上手各种不同领域的人，再给他一点时间去训练、去跟人聊、去补齐专业度、做一些练习，他其实会干得相当不错。我认为大多数领域本质上都挺浅的，一个非常聪明、在少数核心技能上很强的通才，可以很快进入状态。这当然不是对每一个领域都成立。我的感觉是，AI 会发展出越来越好的机制，用来在给定领域里快速获取理解和专业能力。

举个例子，想想 AI 理解一个新代码库有多快。AI 理解新代码库的速度远快于人类，但深度比人类现在能达到的要浅。不过这一点在随时间变好。让我把这个论证展开一点。假设你拿 Fable 5 或 Mythos 5 之类的模型，你想在一个体量极大的代码库里做某种复杂改动。模型会非常快地建立起对这个代码库的某种理解，可能远远用不了一小时，甚至快得多。然后它的理解会稍微进入平台期——它不会达到人类花长得多的时间所能达到的那种深度。

所以大概是这样：AI 一小时能匹敌人类几周的理解，具体取决于代码库到底有多复杂。但它匹敌不了一个在这个代码库上干了两年的人。可是随着时间推移，AI 能匹敌的理解量一直在往上走。看看 [3.7 Sonnet](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-3-7-sonnet) 或 [3.5 Sonnet](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-3-5-sonnet)，那时候可能只相当于理解代码库一天的水平。

但现在 AI 在为任务构建上下文这件事上强多了。你可以说：「Mythos，我要你真正吃透这个代码库，然后实现这个功能。」它会派出一大堆 sub-agent，这些 sub-agent 会把一堆东西翻个遍，把大量上下文带回来，然后它再去查证几件事。它做得算不上惊艳，但速度真的很快，而且效果相当不错。

而且我不难想象怎么把 AI 训练得在这项任务上越来越强。「在一个很大的代码库里以某种合理方式实现一个非常复杂的功能」这件事极易验证，那就可以成为 AI 持续改进的抓手。同理，还有一项更宽泛的技能：快速理解上下文，让一堆不同的 AI 并行学习，再把结果合并到一起。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

I think there seems to be a crux here, which I think is just an empirical question we’ll see. How good is the transfer between getting really, really good at understanding the situation, getting up to speed, making progress over long periods in verifiable domains — which the AIs are obviously getting way, way better at really fast — to, “Okay, go talk to the president and convince him to do X thing.” Or, “You’re now in charge of Google. You must make Google a much more profitable company this quarter.”

**Ryan Greenblatt**

Let me try to spell out a few more arguments that are maybe relevant. One thing is, when looking at how the AIs have improved at essay writing… Let’s talk about that a little bit. You can get some data even on these domains. AIs will be able to get some data even on these domains when on a very fast progress trajectory. Maybe it’s hard to build a verifiable environment for “was your essay really good according to humans?” But you can do a bit of that. You can do some training. You can do some online training. The AIs will be able to do some online training based on real-world stuff. They’ll be able to have evals. They’ll be able to sample that. You can scale up the cadence at which you do this.

The second thing is that in practice, when I just look at the transfer, it seems okay. I think the AIs have in fact improved a bunch at non-verifiable domains, and it’s hard to point to domains that are really hard to verify on which the amount of improvement between GPT-4 and Mythos hasn’t been pretty high in practice. Now, that doesn’t mean that Mythos is better than the best humans or something. It can still be significantly worse than typical human professionals at some aspect of their job while still being way better than GPT-4, which was not even close.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

我觉得这里似乎有个关键分歧点，而它大概就是个我们迟早会看到答案的经验问题：从「极其擅长理解处境、快速进入状态、在可验证领域里长时间持续推进」——这方面 AI 显然正在飞快变强——迁移到「好，去跟总统谈谈，说服他做 X 这件事」，或者「现在 Google 归你管了，你必须让 Google 这个季度的利润高得多」，这中间的迁移到底有多好？

**Ryan Greenblatt**

让我再摆几个可能相关的论证。第一点是，看看 AI 在写文章这件事上的进步……我们稍微聊聊这个。哪怕在这些领域，你也能拿到一些数据。在快速进步的轨道上，AI 在这些领域里也能拿到一些数据。也许「人类觉得你这篇文章真的好吗」很难构建成可验证环境，但你可以做一点。你可以做一些训练，可以做一些在线训练。AI 将能基于真实世界的东西做一些在线训练，能有 evals，能对它做采样，而且你可以把做这件事的节奏放大。

第二点是，实际去看迁移效果，好像还行。我认为 AI 在不可验证领域上确实进步了不少，而且很难指出哪个「真的很难验证」的领域里，GPT-4 到 Mythos 的进步幅度在实践中不算高。当然，这不代表 Mythos 就比最顶尖的人类强。它完全可能在典型人类专业人士工作的某些方面仍然差不少，同时又比 GPT-4 强得多——GPT-4 那时候根本不在一个量级上。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

So we’re talking about how much progress has come from data versus algorithmic progress over the last few years. That reminds me, I’m actually running an experiment with this with [Jerry Han](https://jerryhan60.github.io/), who’s still a college student. What we’re basically doing to evaluate how much progress is coming from data versus algorithms is training the best algorithmic recipe from 2019 till now with the best data from the 2026 data file, and then also training the different data files going back from 2019 to 2026 with the current best algorithmic recipe.

I think that will be interesting. I’m curious if you want to pre-register what amount of compute multipliers are coming from one versus the other.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

We need to be pretty careful with what we mean when we say the word data. I was trying to be pretty careful to distinguish between scaling up spending on getting human experts to label data, or scaling up the amount of human expert-labeled data. The reason why we have a better [pre-training](https://www.databricks.com/blog/llm-pre-training-and-custom-llms) data set now versus in 2019 is not because people are spending way more money getting human experts to type up data that the AIs are then trained on.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

我们在聊的是，过去这几年的进步里有多少来自数据、多少来自算法进步。这让我想起来，我其实正在跟 [Jerry Han](https://jerryhan60.github.io/) 一起做一个实验，他还是个大学生。我们做的事情基本上是：为了评估进步里有多少来自数据、多少来自算法，我们把 2019 年到现在每一年的最佳算法配方，都用 2026 年的最佳数据文件训一遍；反过来，也把 2019 到 2026 年的各个数据文件，都用当前最佳的算法配方训一遍。

我觉得结果会挺有意思的。我很好奇你想不想先押个注：两边各贡献了多少 compute multiplier（算力乘数）？

**Ryan Greenblatt**

我们说「数据」这个词的时候得非常小心。我一直很谨慎地区分两件事：加大投入去请人类专家标注数据，或者说扩大人类专家标注数据的量。我们今天的 [pre-training](https://www.databricks.com/blog/llm-pre-training-and-custom-llms)（预训练）数据集比 2019 年好，原因并不是大家花了多得多的钱请人类专家去敲出数据来喂给 AI。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

Partially.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

I think it’s not much of it. I think it’s very little of the pre-training data improvements. I do mean pre-training. We should maybe talk separately about [mid-training](https://vintagedata.org/blog/posts/what-is-mid-training) and [post-training](https://pytorch.org/blog/a-primer-on-llm-post-training/). But I think the vast majority of pre-training data improvements are from science on better understanding what data sets are good and schleppy labor on figuring out how to filter down.

So my view is that improvements of the form of, like, [OpenWebText](https://github.com/Skylion007/openwebtext) to [FineWeb](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceFW/fineweb), that improvement is better described as an algorithmic improvement of the sort that you can study with some [GPUs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics_processing_unit), and you don’t need human expert data to do that. Now, there’s a different effect which we could talk about, which is that maybe the internet in 2026 is more of a fertile ground for training data than the internet in 2018. There’s also been an effect where there are just more humans posting on the internet, so there’s more data to harvest. My sense is that that effect is going to be quite a bit smaller than the effect of humans knowing better how to curate the data, having better scrapes, knowing how to process those scrapes better — this sort of thing.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

This is more like automated engineering and automated R&D.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

That’s right.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

That makes sense.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

In some sense, the thing you would want to look at is: we’re going to do two post-training pipelines. You have one post-training pipeline where Mythos 5 builds a post-training pipeline, but it only has access to internet data plus a tiny amount of human experts, but it has the best current methods. You have another one where Mythos has access to the shitty post-training methods we had in 2024 but with a shit ton of human experts. Again, both have the internet data. My sense is that the current methods without many human experts will actually do quite well.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

Interesting.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

It’s a bit messy though, because can Mythos get something that’s more capable than Mythos? You might need to be a bit thoughtful on what model it is that you’re post-training.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

部分是吧。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

我觉得占比不大。我认为在预训练数据的改进里，这部分占比非常小。我说的确实是 pre-training。[mid-training](https://vintagedata.org/blog/posts/what-is-mid-training)（中期训练）和 [post-training](https://pytorch.org/blog/a-primer-on-llm-post-training/)（后训练）也许应该另外聊。但我认为预训练数据的绝大部分改进，来自「搞清楚什么样的数据集才是好数据集」这门科学，以及「怎么把数据过滤下来」这类又脏又累的 schleppy labor（苦力活）。

所以我的看法是，像从 [OpenWebText](https://github.com/Skylion007/openwebtext) 到 [FineWeb](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceFW/fineweb) 这种改进，更应该被描述成一种算法改进——那种你拿几块 [GPU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics_processing_unit) 就能研究的改进，不需要人类专家数据。当然还有另外一个效应可以聊：也许 2026 年的互联网，比 2018 年的互联网更适合当训练数据的沃土。还有一个效应是，往互联网上发东西的人变多了，所以可收割的数据也更多。我的感觉是，这个效应会比另一个效应小不少——那个效应是，人类更懂怎么筛选数据、有更好的抓取、更懂怎么处理这些抓取结果，诸如此类。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

这更像是自动化工程和自动化研发。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

没错。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

有道理。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

某种意义上，你真正该看的实验是这样：我们跑两条后训练流水线。一条是 Mythos 5 来搭后训练流水线，但它只能用互联网数据加极少量人类专家，不过它有当下最好的方法。另一条是 Mythos 只有我们 2024 年那些烂方法，但配上海量人类专家。两边都有互联网数据。我的感觉是，「当前方法 + 很少人类专家」这一条其实会表现相当好。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

有意思。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

不过这事有点乱，因为 Mythos 能搞出比 Mythos 更强的东西吗？你可能得仔细想想，你到底是在对哪个模型做后训练。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

What is your view on what is the least verifiable part of AI R&D?

**Ryan Greenblatt**

The least verifiable, probably making calls on large experiments. The thing that I think is most likely to be the bottleneck — in terms of the AIs being really good at verifiable domains but not at doing the actual thing — is just big experiments where you only get a few tries. Well, “a few” is maybe a bit understated. Historically R&D has been driven by doing near-frontier-scale experiments. That has been pretty important, actually doing the one big training run where you decide exactly what to include.

There’s a bunch of ways that the AIs can make that more verifiable. They can have better science of exactly what to predict. They can scale down their frontier-scale training runs to a point where they can study that scale more aggressively, at some one-time hit to compute cost. If people wanted to, a thing you can always do is train smaller models so that you can run more rounds. I think we have seen this.

One reason why the AIs have been scaled up less than you would have otherwise expected — and, for example, cost per token hasn’t increased as much as you might have thought — is because there is a benefit to doing more of your work at small scale, where you can run more training runs and get more cycles in. So you’re not leaning as hard on one big, really important training run.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

你觉得 AI 研发里最不可验证的环节是什么？

**Ryan Greenblatt**

最不可验证的，大概是对大型实验做判断。我认为最可能成为瓶颈的地方——即「AI 在可验证领域很强，但在真正做那件事上不行」——就是那种你只有寥寥几次机会的大实验。说「几次」可能还说轻了。历史上研发一直是靠做接近前沿规模的实验推动的，那件事其实相当重要：真的跑一次大训练，而且要精确决定里面放什么。

AI 有若干办法让这件事变得更可验证。它们可以把「到底该预测什么」这门科学做得更好；可以把前沿规模的训练缩小到某个尺度，从而更激进地研究那个尺度，代价是一次性的算力损失。如果有人想这么干，你随时可以做的一件事就是训更小的模型，好让你能多跑几轮。我觉得这一点我们已经看到了。

AI 被放大的程度不如你原本预期的一个原因——比如说每 token 成本涨得没你想的那么多——就是因为把更多工作放在小规模上是有好处的：你能跑更多次训练，拿到更多迭代周期。这样你就不必那么依赖某一次又大又关键的训练。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

I just want to unpack a couple of things for the audience. The thing you’re pointing out is that the price per token has not increased that much since 2024 or 2023.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

GPT-4 was, I don’t know, like $30 per million output tokens? Mythos is like $50 per million output tokens.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

Right. So the thing you’re trying to explain is, “How can it be that we’re in this era of scaling — and so bigger models should be more expensive to serve — but the token price is not increasing?” You’re suggesting that we’ve increased active parameters slower than you would have naively assumed because people just want to make fast progress on training models. You do that by training smaller models faster.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

There’s a complicated mix of factors. My view is more that people have done a bunch of big training runs that did not go that well. There’s [GPT-4.5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPT-4.5), which famously people at OpenAI thought was a bit of a bust. I think there are some rumors that there were a bunch of other training runs people have done that were a bit of a bust. Part of it is that I think there’s just a bunch of details in actually getting that right.

So it makes sense to do more of the work at smaller scale and just eat the fact that you’re taking a hit on final performance in order to be able to quickly iterate. Train more models faster and therefore learn better, and also be able to have a smarter ultimate production model. This is not the only effect. There’s also the fact that RL benefits more from small models. There’s a bunch of things going on. But I do think that, in fact, people are making trade-offs towards the side of faster iteration times because of algorithmic progress being so fast.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

我想为听众把几件事拆开讲讲。你指出的是，每 token 的价格从 2024 年或 2023 年到现在其实没涨多少。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

GPT-4 大概是每百万输出 token 30 美元？Mythos 大概是每百万输出 token 50 美元。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

对。所以你想解释的问题是：「我们明明处在一个 scaling 的时代——更大的模型服务成本应该更高——可 token 价格怎么没涨？」你的说法是，我们提升 active parameters（激活参数）的速度比你天真设想的要慢，因为大家就是想在训模型上快速取得进展，而做到这一点的办法就是更快地训更小的模型。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

这里面因素混杂得比较复杂。我的看法更偏向于：大家做过一堆结果并不好的大训练。有 [GPT-4.5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPT-4.5)，众所周知 OpenAI 内部觉得它有点算失败。也有传闻说还有一堆别的训练跑得不太行。部分原因是，要真正把这件事做对，中间有一大堆细节。

所以，把更多工作放到更小规模上，并且接受「最终性能上吃点亏」以换取快速迭代，这是说得通的。训更多模型、训得更快，于是学到更多，最终还能得到一个更聪明的生产模型。这不是唯一的效应。还有一个事实是 RL 从小模型上获益更多。有一堆因素在起作用。但我确实认为，正因为算法进步太快，大家实际上是在往「更快迭代」那一侧做权衡。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

It seems to me that a big source of why these big training runs have failed, at least from rumors, is just very subtle bugs that are really hard to track down.

But the TL;DR is, how good will the AIs be at avoiding and finding these kinds of mistakes? They might get really good at engineering and being trained to avoid bugs. Basically the opposite of the slop world we live in now, or are living in less and less over time.

But then there’s also the question of, “Can they do the analysis to find the right experiment to run to identify what is going wrong with the training run right now?” That seems to be very bottlenecked by the taste of extremely few humans. My assumption is [GDM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_DeepMind) is going through this right now, where humans are trying to figure out what is wrong with the training pipeline.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

There’s a rumor that right after [Noam Shazeer](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/jeff-dean-and-noam-shazeer) joined GDM, which he’s now left, they had a new really good training run, and the reason why is that Noam Shazeer just looked at their code base and found a bunch of bugs, because he just knew where to look.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

在我看来，这些大训练失败的一个主要来源——至少从传闻看——就是那些极其隐蔽、极难定位的 bug。

不过一句话概括就是：AI 在避免和发现这类错误上会有多强？它们可能会在工程上变得非常强，并被训练成避免 bug，基本上是我们现在所处的这个 slop（低质糊弄）世界的反面——而这个世界正在随时间慢慢褪去。

但还有另一个问题：「它们能不能做那种分析，找出该跑哪个实验，来定位当下这次训练到底哪里出了问题？」这件事似乎极度受制于极少数人类的品味。我的猜测是 [GDM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_DeepMind) 现在正在经历这个阶段，人类在试图搞清楚训练流水线哪里不对。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

有个传闻是，[Noam Shazeer](https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/jeff-dean-and-noam-shazeer) 刚加入 GDM 之后（他现在已经离开了），他们有一次训练跑得特别好，原因就是 Noam Shazeer 看了一眼他们的代码库，揪出了一堆 bug——因为他知道该往哪儿看。

bilingual.en:
My sense is that training AIs to find bugs is going to be one of the easier tasks to train AIs on, because most of these bugs we’re talking about can probably be demonstrated without that much compute. Probably you’ll get pretty good transfer from pointing out other types of bugs at smaller scale. So then you can RL AIs that look at this overall complicated training situation and point out cases where there’s an important bug, and then fix that.

This is a pretty verifiable task. It’s not arbitrarily verifiable, because maybe often to demonstrate the bug you might need to do a moderate-scale compute experiment where you spin up the whole distributed infrastructure and then run it. But oftentimes I think you’ll be able to demonstrate it pretty convincingly at smaller scale in a way which you could actually train on.

I think it wouldn’t be very surprising if right now people have RL environments where they introduce a subtle bug into some training recipe, train the AI to point out the subtle bug, and then have a rubric where they’re like, “Did it actually find the right bug?” That seems very doable, and there’s a bunch of things you could do along these lines that I think would work reasonably well. So on that specific point, I think it’s doable.

Then the main thing is there’s other intuition about which exact large-scale de-risking experiments you need to run. How should you orient them? How should you pick hyperparameters in uncertain cases, or things that are analogous to hyperparameters? That’s the thing the AIs might most struggle with. But I currently expect there’ll be enough transfer if you train on all these different environments, that the AIs will be good at that domain.

I should be clear, I also think the AIs will transfer to other domains. There are going to be the domains the AIs are by far the best at, then domains where they’re somewhat less good, and domains where they’re quite a bit less good. But I think we still see transfer to everything. It’s really hard for me to think of examples of cognitive tasks humans do where we’re not seeing some transfer from AI improving.
bilingual.zh:
我的感觉是，训练 AI 找 bug 会是比较容易训的任务之一，因为我们在说的这些 bug，大多数大概不需要多少算力就能复现。而且从更小规模上指出其他类型的 bug，很可能会有不错的迁移。于是你就可以 RL 一批 AI，让它们看着这一整套复杂的训练状况，指出哪里存在重要的 bug，然后修掉。

这是一个相当可验证的任务。它不是任意可验证的，因为要复现那个 bug，你有时可能需要做一个中等规模的算力实验，把整套分布式基础设施拉起来再跑。但我认为很多时候，你能在更小规模上相当有说服力地复现它，而且是以一种你真的可以拿来训练的方式。

如果现在已经有人做了这样的 RL 环境——往某个训练配方里塞进一个隐蔽 bug，训练 AI 把这个隐蔽 bug 指出来，再配一套评分标准问「它是不是真找到了那个 bug？」——我一点都不会意外。这看起来非常可行，而且沿着这条路线还有一堆做法我认为都能work得相当不错。所以就这个具体点而言，我觉得是可行的。

那么剩下的主要问题就是：还有一类直觉，关于你到底需要跑哪些大规模的去风险实验。该怎么设计它们？在不确定的情况下该怎么选超参数，或者选那些类超参数的东西？这才是 AI 可能最吃力的地方。但我目前预期，如果你在所有这些不同环境上训练，会有足够的迁移，让 AI 在这个领域也变得很强。

我要说清楚，我也认为 AI 会迁移到其他领域。会有一些领域 AI 遥遥领先，一些领域它们没那么强，还有一些领域它们差不少。但我认为我们仍然能看到对所有领域的迁移。我很难想出哪个人类做的认知任务，是我们完全看不到 AI 进步带来迁移的。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

So let’s step back and package this whole story. I think people can probably follow along with this story. We have GPT-7.5 trained on a bunch of environments, where it’s not only in general becoming a better AI, but specifically we’re training it to do AI R&D better. It’s making GPT-2 size runs that are better at playing video games that require sample efficiency or online learning or whatever other capabilities.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

Another thing that’s really important is you don’t just do GPT-2 sized runs, you also do small fine-tuning runs on GPT-6. As in, you have GPT-2, and you can do full pre-trains of GPT-2, and then you can do small post-training or mid-training or whatever runs on GPT-6. And then you can do a small number of experiments that are actually at frontier scale, but you do a bit of online training or something.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

What do you mean by “do online training” on that?

**Ryan Greenblatt**

Another thing we can do is take GPT-7.5, and presumably in the course of GPT-7.5’s work, it’s running a bunch of experiments at varying scale that are actually on the critical path for AI R&D. For many of those things you’ll be able to get a sense after the fact of whether or not it did a good job.

So it did some post-training experiment where it was trying to figure out whether some method actually works. In some cases you’ll be like, “Whoa, it found this kickass method, it totally de-risked it, it totally worked.” And then you can reinforce that.

One thing you could do would be to convert the experiment it just ran into an RL environment based on production data and then train on that. Or you could potentially just literally take the rollouts that found that and do some sort of [off-policy RL](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/on-policy-vs-off-policy-methods-reinforcement-learning/), or you could do some [on-policy RL](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/on-policy-vs-off-policy-methods-reinforcement-learning/) with some production data.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

那我们退一步，把整个故事打包起来。我觉得大家应该能跟得上这个故事。我们有一个 GPT-7.5，在一堆环境上训练过，它不只是总体上变成一个更好的 AI，我们还专门训练它把 AI 研发做得更好。它在跑 GPT-2 规模的训练，让模型更擅长玩那些需要样本效率、在线学习或者别的什么能力的电子游戏。

**Ryan Greenblatt**

还有一件非常重要的事：你不只是跑 GPT-2 规模的训练，你还会在 GPT-6 上做小规模微调。也就是说，你有 GPT-2，可以对 GPT-2 做完整预训练；然后你可以在 GPT-6 上做小规模的后训练或中期训练之类的跑法。再然后，你可以做少量真正处在前沿规模的实验，但只做一点在线训练之类的东西。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

你说在那上面「做在线训练」是什么意思？

**Ryan Greenblatt**

我们还能做的一件事是：拿 GPT-7.5，而在 GPT-7.5 干活的过程中，它多半正在跑一堆不同规模的实验，这些实验实际上就处在 AI 研发的关键路径上。对其中很多事情，你事后是能判断出它做得好不好的。

比如它做了某个后训练实验，想搞清楚某个方法到底有没有用。有些情况下你会说：「哇，它找到了一个牛逼方法，把风险彻底排掉了，完全奏效。」那你就可以强化这一次。

一种做法是，把它刚跑完的那个实验、基于生产数据转化成一个 RL 环境，然后在上面训练。或者你也可以干脆直接把找到这个结果的 rollouts 拿来做某种 [off-policy RL](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/on-policy-vs-off-policy-methods-reinforcement-learning/)，或者用一些生产数据做 [on-policy RL](https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/machine-learning/on-policy-vs-off-policy-methods-reinforcement-learning/)。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

Basically the thing you’re suggesting is: there’s the small-scale stuff where you’re teaching the AI to get better at AI R&D taste, but you’re discarding the actual “things it found”. Then it actually does real R&D in the practice of trying to become better at AI R&D, and you’re like, “This is a pretty cool thing that you discovered. Let’s actually also use this in production in the future, and teach you how to use it in production.”

**Ryan Greenblatt**

That’s right.

**Dwarkesh Patel**

But stepping back, GPT-7.5 becomes GPT-8 as a result of all this AI R&D training and just generally becoming smarter. Then it helps you build GPT-9. Another very important thing has to happen, which is maybe the thing I’m most skeptical of. GPT-8 has figured out how to make it so… GPT-9, as intelligent as it is… Humans currently, AI researchers, try their stuff, and they’re like, “Okay, but we trained GPT-4.5 and it wasn’t good.” It required real-world feedback or some evaluation of trying to use the model in production. Then they were like, “It wasn’t that good, and we’re not going to ship it.”

So GPT-8 needs this ability to see how good the transfer is to all these other things you’re talking about — like being really good at Texas politics, or really good at running a business, et cetera — which is not a production environment and, in fact, cannot be a containerized environment given the nature of the task. As the agents get longer and longer horizon, the short-horizon things you can containerize are like, “Okay, code this up or whatever.” Extremely long-horizon things — “Go run a successful business, go have a profitable day in the markets, go negotiate a trade deal” — these things are actually very hard to containerize.

So I think it’s very plausible that it’s very hard for GPT-8 to figure out how to make this transfer to those environments. It may just not be in the nature of the training. Or maybe by default, training just doesn’t generalize in that way.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

你说的基本上是这个意思：有一部分是小规模的东西，你在教 AI 提升 AI 研发的品味，但你把它「实际找到的东西」丢掉了。然后它在「让自己更擅长 AI 研发」的实践中，真的做了真实研发，于是你说：「你发现的这东西挺酷的。我们以后在生产里也真的用上它吧，并且教你怎么在生产里用。」

**Ryan Greenblatt**

没错。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

但退一步看，GPT-7.5 经过这一整套 AI 研发训练、以及总体上变得更聪明，成了 GPT-8。然后它帮你造 GPT-9。这中间还必须发生另一件非常重要的事，而这大概是我最怀疑的一环。GPT-8 已经想明白了怎么让……GPT-9，无论它多聪明……现在的人类 AI 研究员会去试他们的东西，然后说：「好吧，可我们训了 GPT-4.5，它不行。」这需要真实世界的反馈，或者某种把模型放到生产里试用的评估。然后他们说：「它没那么好，我们不发布了。」

所以 GPT-8 需要有这种能力：看清楚迁移到你说的那些别的东西上到底有多好——比如非常擅长德州政治，或者非常擅长经营一门生意，等等——而这些既不是生产环境，而且鉴于任务本身的性质，也根本没法做成容器化环境。随着 agent 的时间跨度越来越长，那些你能容器化的短跨度任务就是「好，把这个东西写出来」之类的。而极长跨度的事情——「去把一门生意经营成功、去在市场上做出赚钱的一天、去谈成一份贸易协定」——这些东西其实非常难容器化。

所以我觉得很有可能，GPT-8 很难搞清楚怎么让这种迁移发生到那些环境上。它可能就不在训练的本性里。或者说，默认情况下训练就是不会以那种方式泛化。

bilingual.en:
**Ryan Greenblatt**

So a concern you might have is: we train GPT-8, and GPT-8 is again better at all the R&D tasks that we can measure but is not good at some downstream tasks we care about. I have a few points.

First, I expect that if you do the obvious thing, you will get pretty good transfer. You’ll be able to hold out some of the obvious stuff you’re doing. When I say “do the obvious thing”, I just mean training on a wide variety of different environments where the AI has to accomplish weird objectives in all kinds of different cases and learn about what’s going on.

The second point is you’ll be able to get some feedback with some environments. You can get a sense of what it can do over the course of a few days in various different contexts. If it’s transferring to really out-of-distribution things, like doing some weird task in a few days in the real world, maybe you think it’s also transferring to doing things over a longer time period or whatever. I think the details of that vary though.

The third thing is that for the world to be radically transformed, it is sufficient for the AIs to be really good at R&D. If the AIs were really, really good at chip R&D, building [fabs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_fabrication_plant), orchestrating factories, designing robots, operating robots, and also at AI R&D — developing AIs for new downstream domains with whatever data is available — I think that would already be a pretty crazy situation. From there, you can get what we might call an [industrial explosion](https://www.forethought.org/research/the-industrial-explosion), where the AIs are building out way, way more compute. Also, maybe you’re already in a regime where AIs are doing huge amounts of R&D that humans have a hard time understanding.
bilingual.zh:
**Ryan Greenblatt**

所以你可能会有的一个担忧是：我们训出 GPT-8，它在所有我们能度量的研发任务上又一次变强了，但在我们真正在意的某些下游任务上并不行。我有几点回应。

第一，我预期如果你做那件显而易见的事，你会得到相当不错的迁移。你可以把一部分显而易见的东西留作 holdout。我说「做显而易见的事」，意思就是在种类极其广泛的环境上训练，让 AI 在各种各样奇怪的情形下完成奇怪的目标，并且搞清楚状况。

第二点是，你可以从一些环境里拿到反馈。你能大致看出它在不同场景下、在几天的时间里能做成什么。如果它能迁移到真正 out-of-distribution（分布外）的事情上，比如在真实世界里花几天做某个古怪任务，那也许你会认为它同样能迁移到更长时间跨度的事情上。不过我觉得这里的细节因情况而异。

第三点是，要让世界被彻底改变，AI 只要在研发上非常强就够了。如果 AI 在芯片研发、建 [fab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semiconductor_fabrication_plant)（晶圆厂）、调度工厂、设计机器人、操作机器人上都非常非常强，同时在 AI 研发上也很强——用手头能拿到的任何数据为新的下游领域开发 AI——我觉得那已经是一个相当疯狂的局面了。从那里出发，你就能得到我们可以称之为 [industrial explosion](https://www.forethought.org/research/the-industrial-explosion)（工业爆炸）的东西，AI 会把算力建得多得多得多。而且，那时你可能已经处在一个 AI 在做海量研发、而人类很难理解这些研发的状态里了。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

So the thing you’re pointing out is that there probably will be this transfer outside of these environments to maneuvering around in courtrooms and the halls of Congress and business boardrooms.

**Ryan Greenblatt**

Given some effort to improve the transfer and blah, blah, blah, blah.

所以你指出的是，很可能确实会有那种迁移——从这些环境迁移到在法庭、国会走廊和企业董事会里周旋。

前提是花了一些功夫去改进迁移之类之类的。

**Dwarkesh Patel**

But even if there’s not, what you’re suggesting is: if you wanted to transform the world of the 18th century, you might care about how well you can navigate [Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom) or something. So you’re suggesting that at this time, AI companies are also working on robotics progress, which is very commingled with AI research progress. **Ryan Greenblatt**

Yeah, that’s basically right. My perspective is that if AIs are sufficiently good at R&D, including hardware R&D, robots, whatever, then they can radically transform the world, even if they’re not that good at playing politics. Also, we’re in a pretty dangerous situation, because the AIs might be doing huge amounts of really hard-to-understand R&D, building out basically the whole economy of the future, and we may not understand what’s going on in there.
bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

但就算没有那种迁移，你的意思是：如果你想改变 18 世纪的世界，你可能会在意自己在 [Westminster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_United_Kingdom)（英国议会）里周旋得怎么样。但你可能在意的另一件事是：「你能不能直接开始造蒸汽船、造他妈的电报、造 [Maxim gun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maxim_gun)（马克沁机枪）之类的东西？」如果你能在这方面做到极强，你在 18 世纪就能是个他妈的超级变革性的存在。你不一定非得特别擅长去说服亨利国王信什么鬼话。我这中世纪历史扯得一塌糊涂，我猜那会儿亨利并不是国王。不过总之，这就是你的意思。

所以你的意思是，在这个时点上，AI 公司同时也在推进机器人技术，而这跟 AI 研究的进展是高度纠缠的。所以如果你能造更多机器人，如果这些机器人由更好的、达到人类水平的 AI 来操作……人类水平的 [teleoperation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teleoperation)（遥操作）在机器人上其实效果相当好，我们只是还没有人类水平的机器人模型而已。所以你的意思是，如果我们做到了这一点——如果 AI 在芯片设计等等可验证的东西上变得极强，然后又极其擅长建晶圆厂——那就相当于回到 18 世纪说：「行，我不知道你们在议会里吵吵什么，但我有一堆蒸汽船和一堆马克沁机枪。」

**Ryan Greenblatt**

对，基本就是这样。我的看法是，如果 AI 在研发上足够强，包括硬件研发、机器人之类的，那它们就能彻底改造世界，哪怕它们不太擅长玩政治。同时，我们的处境也相当危险，因为 AI 可能在做海量非常难以理解的研发，基本上是在把未来的整个经济体建出来，而我们可能并不明白那里面在发生什么。

bilingual.en:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

Before we move on to the alignment stuff, I think a big source of [FUD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear,_uncertainty,_and_doubt) right now is this realization that this is the way the future is going: extreme [economies of scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economies_of_scale) for the leading labs. The ability to amortize so much intelligence and capabilities across so many different sectors of the economy basically into one model. And not only that, that model will eventually be able to learn from experience.

Right now, it’s happening through a process intermediated by humans, where the humans are trying to basically steal your business. They’re like, “Okay, you can do design at [Figma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figma), or whatever. We’ll get Claude to do that.” Or, “You can do whatever coding agent. We’ll have Claude internalize that capability.” But eventually, that will be a much more automated process.

bilingual.zh:
**Dwarkesh Patel**

在进入对齐话题之前，我觉得现在一大 [FUD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fear,_uncertainty,_and_doubt)（恐惧、不确定与怀疑）的来源，是大家意识到未来正在这样走：领先实验室会拥有极端的 [economies of scale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economies_of_scale)（规模经济）。它们能把如此多的智能和能力，摊销到经济体如此多的不同部门上，而这基本上被压缩进一个模型里。不仅如此，那个模型最终还会能够从经验中学习。

现在这个过程还是由人类居中中介的，人类在试图抢你的生意。他们说：「行，你在 [Figma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figma) 上做设计之类的，我们让 Claude 来干。」或者「你有个什么编码 agent，我们让 Claude 把这个能力内化掉。」但最终，这会变成一个自动化程度高得多的过程。
